svg.aria-label: Diagram: AWS Health now supports resource and account tags in Health events, enriching events with resource tags and account tags so you can view resource tags directly within Health events for supported AWS services, while account-level tags help you categorize and filter events across your organization and enable more granular event filtering in the AWS Health Dashboard and AWS Health API responses. The behaviour that matters is in the EntityAccountFilter reference. The tags filter is a map of tag keys to lists of tag values, a tag matches when its key is in the map and its value is one of the values listed for that key, matching is case sensitive, and the filter matches when at least one key in the map matches. That makes a multi-key filter a union rather than an intersection: a filter naming both an environment key and a cost-centre key returns entities matching either one, which is wider than the conjunction most people intend to write. The filter also does not distinguish the two tag sources: an entity is returned when the tags of the resource, or of the account it belongs to, match, so there is no documented way to filter on resource tags alone, even though the response separates them into a resourceTags map and an accountTags map. When you specify several filters in organizationEntityAccountFilters the tags must be identical in every filter, so one organizational call cannot carry a different tag predicate per account. The retrieval paths also differ: accountTags is a map of account tag key-value pairs for the account that owns the affected entity, and this field is returned only by DescribeAffectedEntitiesForOrganization and is not populated by DescribeAffectedEntities, even though the single-account operation response syntax shows the accountTags key, so a member-account caller reading it gets nothing and no error. Both maps cap at a maximum of 10 items, tag keys at 127 characters and values at 255, and the filter value array holds a maximum of 50 items per key, giving a ceiling of 500 tag values expressible in one filter. For EventBridge, the announcement promises sophisticated routing and handling of Health events based on tag values, but the AWS Health EventBridge schema reference documents affectedEntities as carrying entityValue, lastUpdatedtime and status only and does not document a tag field, so an event pattern should be written against an observed event rather than from the schema page; note also that pagination occurs only on resources and if the 256KB size limit is exceeded for another reason the communication fails. Finally, tag enrichment is not on by default: to enable tag enrichment, visit the AWS Health Dashboard. Calling the AWS Health API requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan and the US East North Virginia Region endpoint.
svg.title: The filter unions its keys, and an account tag matches as if it belonged to the resource
svg.text: The announcement says filter. The reference says how — and it is not an AND.
“account-level tags help you categorize and filter events across your organization, making it easier to
route notifications and automate responses based on your organizational structure.”
The one sentence to read before writing a filter
“Matching is case sensitive, and the filter matches when at least one key in the map matches.”
{ Environment: [prod], CostCenter: [4812] } → prod OR 4812, not prod AND 4812
Adding a second key widens the result set. Narrowing it is your own job, after the call returns.
Two tag sources in, one undifferentiated match
“An entity is returned when the tags of the resource, or of the account it belongs to, match.”
The response splits them into resourceTags and accountTags. The filter does not. An account tagged
Environment=prod matches every entity in it, whatever the resource itself is tagged.
The field that is in the shape and never in the payload
accountTags — “returned only by DescribeAffectedEntitiesForOrganization and is not populated
by DescribeAffectedEntities.”
Its key still appears in the single-account response syntax. Read it from a member account: empty, no error.
THE CEILINGS
tags map max 10 items
values per key max 50 items
key 127 chars value 255 chars
10 x 50 = 500 tag values in one filter.
EVENTBRIDGE: VERIFY, DO NOT ASSUME
The schema reference documents affectedEntities as
entityValue . lastUpdatedtime . status
No tag field is documented there yet.
Write the pattern against an event you captured.
“To enable tag enrichment, visit the AWS Health Dashboard” — it is a step, not a default, and nothing warns you.
An empty tag map on an event is indistinguishable from an untagged resource, a disabled enrichment, and an
unsupported service — the announcement scopes it to “supported AWS services” without listing them.
Health API calls need a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan and the us-east-1 endpoint.
